power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Science without scientists? In defence of human understanding

author.affiliation:
Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence
								University of Cambridge

text.text: Science has two grand goals, producing results and increasing human understanding, which have usually advanced together.

Accelerating science by automating around human limits threatens to decouple them, as AI research output can scale with compute whereas humans can only read and digest new research at the pace biology allows, and some AI-generated results may be too opaque for anyone to follow.
I argue that this could create a comprehension lag, a growing gap between what is discovered and what humans understand.

This lag may begin inside individual labs, as scientists become "commissioners" directing their own teams of AI agents, but could extend to entire fields, as the frontier moves faster than people can follow.

I discuss three costs of a comprehension lag: a loss of control over AI-accelerated research, a loss of capacity as aspects of training and apprenticeship are automated, and a loss of meaning that scientists find in their work.

I then propose five measures to mitigate the comprehension lag, including new research directions for the cognitive and behavioural sciences, and argue that human understanding deserves protecting, both to keep oversight of AI-driven research and as an end in itself.
Curing cancer, solving climate change, reversing ageing.
Industry leaders regularly cite these potential upsides to justify the rapid adoption of AI in research.
Yet science has two goals: producing results and increasing human understanding.
Even if AI delivers all these hoped-for advances, it is worth asking what we are prepared to lose.

Here I argue that AI risks creating a comprehension lag, in which discoveries accumulate faster than people can absorb them, and that human understanding is worth protecting, both to keep oversight of AI-driven research and for its own sake.
An unwritten rule of science funding is that we justify curiosity by promising impact.
The bargain has usually held, because understanding, however abstract, tends to pay off in ways no one anticipated.
When Francisco Mojica became intrigued by regularly spaced repeats in the genome of an archaeon from the salt ponds of Santa Pola, he could not have known that this would lead to CRISPR gene editing.
AI threatens to decouple the two goals, so that innovation no longer depends on advances in human understanding.
AlphaFold, for instance, predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy without supplying an account of how proteins fold.

Most strikingly, in September 2026 OpenAI reported that thousands of AI agents had produced a machine-verified proof of finitetime blowup for the Navier-Stokes equations, potentially resolving one of the Millennium Prize Problems [1].
text.formatted: Most strikingly, in September 2026 OpenAI reported that thousands of AI agents had produced a machine-verified proof of finitetime blowup for the Navier-Stokes equations, potentially resolving one of the Millennium Prize Problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Weeks later, it released 722 mathematics manuscripts at once, some of which experts found incomprehensible.
Terence Tao was among those who warned that such results could settle a problem without building the understanding that would let the field develop further [2].
text.formatted: Terence Tao was among those who warned that such results could settle a problem without building the understanding that would let the field develop further <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: But if the results keep coming, should we care that human understanding is being left behind?
Science is bottlenecked by human limitations.
Humans sleep, take holidays and need time to read and think.
Their expertise is narrow; the Victorian polymath no longer exists.
In contrast, AI systems can work without pause, in their thousands, and draw on expertise from many domains at once.
The uncomfortable truth is that accelerating science with AI means automating around these human bottlenecks.
Few will mourn offloading admin to AI, but automation is unlikely to stop there.
It will encroach on parts of research closest to our identity as scientists: reading and writing papers, designing studies, planning research agendas and sharing ideas.
There is also competitive pressure to automate.
Every AI-written summary, code repository or slide deck saves its user time, but as everyone saves time, the savings are absorbed by demands for more output [3].
text.formatted: Every AI-written summary, code repository or slide deck saves its user time, but as everyone saves time, the savings are absorbed by demands for more output <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Submissions to the ICML machine learning conference roughly doubled in 2026 alone, to nearly 24,000, a rise some attribute partly to AI agents [4].
text.formatted: Submissions to the ICML machine learning conference roughly doubled in 2026 alone, to nearly 24,000, a rise some attribute partly to AI agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Researchers who automate less risk falling behind, and those who automate aggressively risk offloading critical portions of their own work.
As capabilities improve, declining to automate will start to look like an ideological stance.
When AI systems write better articles and suggest better ideas than we can, do we stick to our own?
Or do we put our name on the paper and add a suitably calibrated AI-use statement to the acknowledgements?
Humans still add irreplaceable value at many points in research.

Nevertheless, holding on to these niches resembles the theological "God of the gaps" argument: gaps in AI capabilities are taken as evidence of humanity's enduring value, even as they shrink with each model release.
We buy productivity by automating around human speed limits.
The cost is that authors may not deeply understand parts of their own research: the rationale, the experimental design, the assumptions behind the analyses.
AI systems can check their work, and the research itself may be impeccable, but the authors' understanding of it lags behind.
This lag resembles what Unceta et al. [3] call "epistemic debt": the gap between what authors present and what they can defend.
text.formatted: This lag resembles what Unceta et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> call "epistemic debt": the gap between what authors present and what they can defend.

text.text: Yet even if every author repaid their own debt by fully internalising their AI-assisted work, a wider comprehension lag would remain.
This wider lag concerns our collective understanding.
Science has long relied on a division of cognitive labour, but until now, each result was usually understood by someone.
Some results, like AlphaFold's predictions, may be too complex and opaque for any human to follow.
More broadly, the frontier may simply move too fast for humans to keep up.
As publication accelerates, peer review may become strained and come to rely, openly or covertly, on AI.
A shrinking share of papers may be read and reflected on deeply by a human.
AI systems will read them and build on them in their next projects.
Research output will scale with compute, whereas human reading proceeds at the pace biology allows.
The gap between the scientific frontier and human understanding could keep widening.
Humans would trail behind, hearing reports of discoveries made by AI at the frontier.
Even this assumes that scientists engage deeply with their own research.

Scientists may instead accept the role of "commissioners": setting agendas, directing AI agents working around the clock and watching the results come in, with only a high-level understanding of the work.
The lag would then begin inside their own labs.

Behavioural science is already moving in this direction as foundation models can simulate participants' choices across a wide range of experiments [5], and as AI agents become more successful at automated psychological research.
text.formatted: Behavioural science is already moving in this direction as foundation models can simulate participants' choices across a wide range of experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, and as AI agents become more successful at automated psychological research.

text.text: A recent study showed agents could design experiments, recruit participants online, and propose cognitive models that fit the data better than established ones [6].
text.formatted: A recent study showed agents could design experiments, recruit participants online, and propose cognitive models that fit the data better than established ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The authors, however, questioned whether the models, which were selected for predictive fit, would provide satisfying explanations for human psychologists.
A growing comprehension lag would carry at least three costs: to our control over AI systems, to our capacity to understand, and to the meaning we find in doing science.
The most serious risk is loss of control.

One response to the lag is to have AI teach us the latest developments, but relying on AI systems to summarise and explain new findings puts us on the wrong side of a dependent relationship, and effective oversight becomes very hard.
Even a well-intentioned AI tutor that glosses over difficult concepts may produce illusions of understanding, in which people believe they grasp a topic they understand only superficially [7].
text.formatted: Even a well-intentioned AI tutor that glosses over difficult concepts may produce illusions of understanding, in which people believe they grasp a topic they understand only superficially <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: A misaligned system, or one aligned to the wishes of a small group, might hide or distort parts of its explanations without our noticing.
AI research and development is where this risk is most acute.
Frontier AI companies are explicitly aiming to automate their own research.
If each generation of AI systems increasingly builds the next, progress could accelerate in an "intelligence explosion", compressing years of advances into months [8].
text.formatted: If each generation of AI systems increasingly builds the next, progress could accelerate in an "intelligence explosion", compressing years of advances into months <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Even partial automation is risky.
Models are "grown" through training, and no one fully understands how they work.

Automating the design choices shaping that training could lead to a loss of understanding that compounds across model generations, and spills over into every field those models are then used to automate.

Even if the alignment problem is solved, we may still lose the capacity to understand, as heavy automation erodes the culture of learning and apprenticeship through which that capacity is passed between generations of scientists.
The relationship between professor and student is partly transactional: the student contributes labour and, in return, acquires the skills of a researcher.
This includes the parts that cannot be learnt from textbooks, such as how to tell when a result is too good to be true, or which questions are worth asking.
Automation breaks this chain.
Student labour can be replaced by AI agents that need no training, and students miss the chance to hone the intuitions that would make them good overseers of those agents.
The next generation may take the reins without knowing what it means to write code from scratch, think through an experimental design unaided or face a blank page.
Some losses will be benign (few of us lament no longer calculating regressions by hand), but others may be critical.
Instead, we might pin our hopes on augmentation: a thought partnership in which humans remain meaningful contributors to research [9].
text.formatted: Instead, we might pin our hopes on augmentation: a thought partnership in which humans remain meaningful contributors to research <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: In competitive chess, human-computer "centaur" teams once outperformed both humans and computers playing alone, but as chess engines improved, the human contribution became negligible.
If science goes the way of chess, human-AI teams may be unable to compete with AI-only research.
Chess remains popular, however, and curiosity may likewise keep many of us doing science for our own understanding.
Humans might become "tinkerers" -hobbyists following idiosyncratic questions down rabbit holes with no need to deliver outcomes.
This may not seem a bad result to some, but it would complete the decoupling of science's two goals: the pursuit of human understanding would no longer shape scientific discovery.
AI-accelerated science may solve many problems sooner.
Nevertheless, human understanding is what allows us to oversee AI-driven research, and it is valuable in itself.
We should think twice before sacrificing it for progress.
Several measures could protect it, and each raises questions about incentives, learning and understanding that the cognitive and behavioural sciences are well placed to answer.
First, we should reward the consolidation of understanding, not merely its production.
Synthesis, replication and explanation of existing work, by humans for humans, should count in hiring and funding decisions.
Second, we should protect training.
A task that is sensibly automated in a lab may be one that a student needs to do by hand, and institutions should decide which learning activities to safeguard.
Third, as written output becomes a poor proxy for understanding, science should place more weight on what researchers can explain unaided [3].
text.formatted: Third, as written output becomes a poor proxy for understanding, science should place more weight on what researchers can explain unaided <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Explaining a topic is known to expose illusions of understanding [10], and conferences and journals could make this routine by discussing a random subset of papers with their authors.
text.formatted: Explaining a topic is known to expose illusions of understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, and conferences and journals could make this routine by discussing a random subset of papers with their authors.

text.text: Fourth, we should study how AI shapes human understanding.
AI tutors are usually judged on the accuracy of their outputs, but their effect on users' understanding is less explored.
This "explanatory uplift", as distinct from the illusion of understanding, should be a key metric for AI developers.
Finally, we should measure the comprehension lag itself.

Anonymous studies of whether experts can explain recent findings in their field, or signals such as how long new results take to reach human-written reviews and teaching, would show whether the lag is growing and where.
Science is, fundamentally, a human invention for understanding the world.
That understanding has brought us new tools and solutions, but it has value of its own.
If we forget that, we risk returning to an age of oracles and seers.
We will come before the gods with our request, and they will give us their answer, however mysterious and cryptic it may seem to us.
